catalog_quote: [Storch 2010: 3] Luwo has three distinctive tonemes, namely high, mid, and low, which may be combined as rising and falling tone sequences. Besides having lexical functions, tone also has grammatical functions, which include the formation of verbal stems, e.g.: ... Stress is also clearly audible in Luwo, but as this phenomenon has not yet been studied in any detail in this language, no generalisation can be made. [Storch 2014: 28, snippet] Luwo has movable stress which is realised in the increased length of the vowel. The nucleus of a stressed syllable is articulated more intensely than that of a non-stressed one. This results in the impression that the respective syllable has more weight. As stress is dynamic, this also causes the impression that vowel length varies in different morphosyntactic contexts. An example is: (2.29) /'twék.twèk./ ['twé:ktwèkh] 'hornbill' /twèk.'twé.gé/ [twèk'twé:yTè] 'hornbills' However, it is possible to demonstrate that syllable weight in stressed syllables, versus phonemic vowel length, differs. Stress moves through affixation of additional grammatical morphemes or construction of compound words, while vowel length is stable, as in the following example, where the stressed prefix /'kar-/ 'home of' is added: (2.30) /'kar.twέk.twèk/ ['kà:rtwéktwèkh] 'hornbill's nest' /'kàr.twèk.twέ.gè/ ['kà:rtwèk'twéyè] ... [Storch 2014: 36, snippet] Stress is not contrastive and therefore there is no criterion for the phonological word either.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (TUFS repository record 7676; image-only, encrypted copy:no, hence the scanned), re-rendered p. 3 at 130 dpi and read the page scan myself. The quoted passage is verbatim on p. 3: the tone paragraph "Luwo has three distinctive tonemes, namely high, mid, and low, which may be combined as rising and falling tone sequences. Besides having lexical functions, tone also has grammatical functions, which include the formation of verbal stems, e.g.:" followed by examples (5.a) transitive stems and (5.b) aspect stems, then the last paragraph of sec. 2 Phonology: "Stress is also clearly audible in Luwo, but as this phenomenon has not yet been studied in any detail in this language, no generalis…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Luwo is a three-tone language (H, M, L, with rising and falling sequences; tone is both lexical and grammatical). The author states that stress is clearly audible but has not been studied, so no rule for its placement is given. Ancillary facts from the same source: roots are always monosyllabic (sec. 3.1.1, p. 4) and affixes are mostly single (C)V suffixes, so any word-level stress would necessarily be near the root.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the source explicitly declines to generalise.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level phonology sketch based on elicited data from Luwo speakers in Khartoum (2000-2007); the statement is about the language in general, not citation forms specifically. Gilley 2004 (OPSL 9, p. 169) independently confirms three level tones for Luwo and says nothing about stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Statement concerns Luwo proper (Jur/Dhe Luwo, ISO lwo, luwo1239) as spoken by consultants in Khartoum from the Wau area; Storch 2010 p. 1 says northern/southern dialect variation is negligible. Thuri (Glottolog: sister language under the Luwo-Thuri node luwo1240) is said to use Luwo materials but is not described here.

sources.note: Comparative orthography overview. Sec. 4 Tone p. 169: 'All the Lwoian languages included here have three level tones and at least some have contour tones on short vowels.. Luwo writes tone on specific words where meaning would otherwise be unclear.' No statement on Luwo stress; the stress remarks (pp. 171-172) concern Shilluk suffixes only.
